name: Tripsacum
visual_status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — 5 photo-led genus panels including verified Uvalde male anthers, female stigmas and mature female joints; no calibrated collar ligule, rhizome or 1 mm detached fruit specimen yet.
fast_fill_note: Tripsacum dactyloides now has a 3-image FAST-FILL gallery covering whole-plant habit and reproductive structure.
look_here_first: ONLY INSTALLED GENUS MEMBER: eastern gamagrass (*Tripsacum dactyloides*). Find the unusually BROAD, strongly midribbed leaves on a large warm-season perennial clump. Most importantly, follow ONE thick corn-related reproductive axis: the densely overlapping upper part contains paired MALE (staminate) spikelets; the LOWER enlarged segmented part carries FEMALE (pistillate) units with protruding purple feathery stigmas. After maturation the lower units harden and can break into bead-like fruit joints. Our source-labelled macro photograph actually shows the upper region, the green lower swollen joints, and purple stigmas, not extruded anthers or hardened detached beads. Do not mix it up with slender big-bluestem turkey-foot racemes, Indiangrass's loose panicle, or invasive Johnsongrass's branching plume. Three separate Jim Conrad 2014 Uvalde original photographs now show TRUE male anthers, female stigmas, and mature tan seed-bearing joints; these are external public-domain teaching views, not proof of measured same-plant microanatomy.

visual_comparison.memory_rule: UPPER male anthers → LOWER female feathery stigmas → ripe tan hard female joints, all part of a thick gamagrass spike; Uvalde photos document separate stages and cannot be presumed one same plant.

comparison_lesson.title: Recognize gamagrass versus big bluestem, Indiangrass, Johnsongrass and corn
comparison_lesson.first_split: Start with reproductive structure: the upper male + lower jointed female portions are part of one continuous Tripsacum flowering axis. That is far stronger than leaf width, color, or a large clump.

rows.photo_evidence: Upper compact green male-region spikelets and lower swollen green female units with purple plumose stigmas visible in same source photo; huge arching clump visible in other photo
rows.distinction: Thick segmented axis with both sexes; mature lower segments become individually detachable hard seed-bearing beads.
rows.what_to_photograph: Fresh intact spike with extruded upper yellow anthers and lower purple stigmas; mature fruit bead with millimeter scale.

comparison_lesson.memory_rule: Gamagrass's purple feather-like projections are FEMALE stigmas; pollen anthers come from the upper staminate flowers and should be distinguished by actual photographed organs.
pitfalls: One photo of leaves only cannot distinguish native gamagrass from coarse nonnative Johnsongrass.
Male and female portions must be located on the SAME intact gamagrass flowering spike, not on separate stems.
A green young female joint is not a mature hard shattering seed; existing photo only shows immature joints.
The purple fluffy stigmas are not stamens or male anthers. Do not draw a false 'anther' arrow on them.
The genus is not globally monotypic: one Tripsacum species is INSTALLED IN THIS LEARNER, not the entire worldwide genus.

what_to_teach_crew: First look for very broad ribbed leaf blades arising in one large bunch; this gets you a gamagrass candidate, not a confirmed ID.
Second find a thick flowering axis. Locate compact male spikelets at the UPPER end and beadlike pistillate units at the LOWER end; label on same photo.
Third distinguish purple branched feathery FEMALE stigmas from staminate pollen anthers (yellow/brown, often absent in our archived flowering image).
Fourth return when lower joints ripen and harden, then photograph a one-seeded detachable segment at mm scale without damaging natural populations.
Finally distinguish johnsongrass open plume, Indiangrass loose panicle and big bluestem slender turkey-foot spikes; check actual reproductive anatomy before a crew-facing species call.
Use new panels 3–5 to compare actual hanging anthers (male), feathery stigmas (female), then ripe tan lower joints. Never call the featherlike stigma an anther or the whole bead a bare seed.
